title: Equidistance Line Finder: The Fair Meeting Line
description: Draw every point that is the same distance from two places with the Equidistance Line Finder — the perpendicular bisector on a real map. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, between New York and Boston the line passes just west of Hartford — Hartford itself is approx. 100.4 miles from New York but 92.4 from Boston, so it sits on Boston's side of fair.
quick_answer: The Equidistance Line Finder draws the line of every point that is exactly the same straight-line distance from two places you choose. It is the perpendicular bisector of the pair, drawn on the real map: stand anywhere on it and neither side has travelled further than the other, geometrically speaking.
steps_intro: Two places, one fairness boundary — draw it instead of arguing about it:

body.t: Two offices, two families, two teams: pick anywhere on the line and the geography is neutral. Towns near the line, not the midpoint alone, become the candidate list — the
calculator gives the centre point itself.
Sales and service territories drawn as equidistance lines need no apology: every customer is served from the nearer base by construction.
Draw equidistance lines between several bases pairwise and you are sketching a Voronoi diagram — the geometry behind coverage maps — one honest line at a time.
The perpendicular bisector stops being a compass-and-ruler ritual when it runs between two cities students know. The 'aha' is that the line is a great circle, not a ruler line.

The midpoint is 41.546, −72.551 in Connecticut. Hartford feels like it should sit on the line — it does not: approx. 100.4 miles to New York against 92.4 to Boston, so the true line runs roughly 4 miles west of the city. Feelings are not measurements; this tool is.

Every point on the drawn line checks out the same way Hartford does not: measure from any point on it to both places and the answers match. Move off it and one side wins immediately — the line is a boundary, not a zone.

faq: Is every point on the line exactly equidistant?
Yes, by construction — that is the definition of the perpendicular bisector on the sphere. The drawn line is the set of points whose distances to your two places are equal.
What is the midpoint used for?

The midpoint is the single point where the line crosses the pair's great-circle path — the fairest single meeting point. The line generalises it: every point on the line is equally fair, just further from both.
Is the line straight on the map?
It is a great circle, so most flat projections bend it slightly. Over city-scale distances the bend is invisible; over continental pairs it becomes part of the lesson.
Does equal distance mean equal travel time?
No — roads differ. The line settles the geographic argument; settle the practical one by testing candidate towns on it with a drive-time tool.
Can I draw lines for three places?

Pairwise — three places make three lines, and where they meet is the point equidistant from all three. For the balanced-centre version, the Geographic Meeting Point Finder computes a centroid instead.
What is this called in mathematics?
The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points — on a sphere, a great circle through the midpoint at right angles to the pair's great circle.
Why does the line extend so far?
Equidistance does not expire with distance: points far away can still be equally far from both places, so the line is drawn across the whole map.
